title: Finite Key Underwater Quantum Key Distribution: Performance Analysis and Improvements
authors: Trevor Thomas, Michael Warnock, Sarah Previte, Benjamin Drozdenko, Walter O. Krawec
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) allows for the establishment of a secret key between two parties, secure against computationally unbounded adversaries. Most experimental and theoretical research in this area, investigates the performance of QKD over fiber or free space channels. A growing body of work, however, has begun to investigate its performance in underwater scenarios. Here, we consider the realistic finite key scenario, and evaluate the simulated performance of two different decoy state protocols. We show that there are certain underwater channels where "simpler" QKD protocols outperform more complex ones. Finally, we also investigate methods to improve QKD performance underwater, specifically looking at classical advantage distillation, which we show can greatly improve the maximal distance supported by QKD underwater.
summary: This paper provides a detailed theoretical analysis of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) performance when transmitting keys underwater. It simulates the finite key regime, accounting for realistic noise sources like ambient light and water attenuation. The study demonstrates that post-processing techniques like Classical Advantage Distillation can significantly boost achievable distances in noisy underwater environments.
main_problem: The paper evaluates Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) performance over realistic underwater channels, moving beyond asymptotic bounds to consider the finite key regime.
main_result: Classical Advantage Distillation (CAD) can significantly improve the maximal supported distance for QKD underwater when ambient light noise is high, although protocol choice and detector efficiency are critical factors.
method: The authors simulate two decoy state protocols in a finite key setting, incorporating detailed models for signal attenuation loss and background noise specific to underwater environments.
model_or_system: The system modeled is quantum communication through an underwater channel using weak coherent sources. The model incorporates Poisson photon statistics, detector imperfections (dark counts, efficiency), and environmental factors like water type and ambient light.
key_observables: Secret key establishment rate ($\ell$ / total signals sent) and the maximal supported distance under various noise conditions.
important_parameters: Attenuation coefficient ($\alpha$), background irradiance ($E_0$), detector efficiency ($\eta$), and the CAD block size ($C$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a weak coherent source, relies on specific mathematical models for attenuation (e.g., exponential decay), and treats post-processing steps like error correction and privacy amplification.
figures_summary: Figures compare key rates using decoy state BB84 protocols with and without CAD under varying environmental conditions; Tables summarize the maximal asymptotic distance based on detector efficiency, light level, and CAD block settings for different water types.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first detailing the physical models for signal attenuation loss over distance, then modeling background noise sources. It culminates in evaluating the protocol performance using finite key derivations, specifically analyzing the benefit of Classical Advantage Distillation (CAD) under varying environmental parameters.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum communication in complex, noisy media (underwater), which is a major open problem in quantum networking and requires advanced understanding of channel capacity estimation beyond simple loss models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Comparing the key-rate of the three (Blue) and the two (Red) decoy state BB84 protocol, for N = 107 rounds (Solid) and N = 108 rounds (Dashed) Here we assume near ideal detector efficiency of 0.9, pure sea water α = 0.043, and low ambient light E0 = 10−3. We note that two decoy outperforms three decoy in this scenario. Black: Asymptotic upper bound.

Fig. 2. Comparing the key-rate of the three (Blue) and the two (Red) decoy state BB84 protocol, for N = 107 rounds (Solid) and N = 108 rounds (Dashed) Here we assume near ideal detector efficiency of 0.9, pure sea water α = 0.043, and heavy overcast, with the sun at the horizon E0 = 10. We note that at N = 108 signals, three decoy outperforms slightly the two decoy protocol.

Fig. 3. Comparing the key-rate of the three (Blue) and the two (Red) decoy state BB84 protocol for N = 108 rounds (Dashed) Here we assume near ideal detector efficiency of 0.9, pure sea water α = 0.043, and lighter overcast E0 = 20. We note that, here, the three decoy state always outperforms, though distances are severely limited. We also note that N = 107 rounds did not produce a positive key-rate for either protocol.

Fig. 4. Comparing the key-rate of the three (Blue) and the two (Red) decoy state BB84 protocol for N = 108 rounds (Dashed) Here we assume near ideal detector efficiency of 0.9, coastal ocean water α = 0.398, and night E0 = 10−3. We note that, here, again, the two decoy state protocol outperforms. We also note that N = 107 rounds did not produce a positive key-rate for either protocol.

Fig. 5. Comparing the key-rate of the three (Blue) and the two (Red) decoy state BB84 protocol, for N = 107 rounds (Solid) and N = 108 rounds (Dashed) Here we assume low detector efficiency of 0.1. As expected, detector efficiency can greatly reduce maximal distances, even at night in ideal water.
